sweep_summary: Hehe (hehe1240) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Möhlig 1969 'Zur prosodologischen Analyse sogenannter Tonsprachen im Bantu' (ZDMG Supplementa I, Teil 3, pp. 1155-1165), is confirmed to exist (DNB table of contents of Teil 3 saved; Bibliotheca Orientalis 27 (1970) contents notice saved) and per Glottolog/Maho deals primarily with Dciriku and only secondarily with Hehe, Chaga and Shi; no open copy exists anywhere reachable (Crossref/OpenAlex/S2/CORE/IA full-text/Google Books/HathiTrust/Halle opendata/BASE all negative or bot-blocked), so it is print-only and its Hehe content (tone vs accent; any stress position) is unread -- priority high for acquisition since tone-vs-accent in Hehe is exactly its topic. A Crossref side-hit, Kähler-Meyer 1963 'Bantu-Tonsprachen und -Nichttonsprachen in Tanganyika' (STUF 16, De Gruyter DOI, paywalled), is a further candidate (medium). The best first-hand stress statement actually read is Velten 1899 p.167 (verified on the page image): word accent on the first stem syllable, with first-stem plus final accent in four-syllable words, accented vowel long -- an early impressionistic description; modern sources (Odden 1988/2005, Kindole 2012 via Ngwasi 2021, all on file from the earlier audit) treat Hehe as a tone language with a penultimate-H rule and give no stress rule. In general the word accent lies on the first stem syllable. In four-syllable words the first stem syllable and the last syllable are stressed, e.g. kifúnguliró 'key', kisámuliró 'comb', etc. Deviations are specially marked.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Literal reading of Velten: word accent on the first syllable of the stem (i.e. after the class prefix), with an additional accent on the final syllable in longer (four-syllable) words; exceptions marked ad hoc with acute accents. Modern first-hand work (Odden 1988; Odden 2005/2013; Odden & Odden 1999 as cited) analyses Kihehe as a tone language: nouns carry lexically selected H patterns (pre-stem-initial, stem-initial, penult, antepenult and combinations; more than one H per word possible), verbs get H by tense-specific rules, e.g. H on a penultimate vowel not immediately preceded by another H, H on the infinitive prefix. Velten's 'Wortton auf der ersten Stammsilbe' most likely records (pre-)stem-initial H tone heard as prominence; no modern source seen makes a stress statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Velten: in four-syllable words both the first stem syllable and the final syllable are 'betont' (kifúnguliró, kisámuliró) -- effectively a second prominence on the final; no primary/secondary ranking given.
new_statements.exceptions: Velten: 'Abweichungen sind besonders gekennzeichnet' -- deviating accents are marked individually in the word lists with an acute.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms elicited in Dar es Salaam (1894ff) from three Hehe women (wives of Mkwawa) held as prisoners, partly through a non-native intermediary; Velten ties vowel length to the accented syllable, whereas modern sources treat Kihehe vowel length as contrastive and prominence as tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Kihehe of the Iringa region = Glottolog hehe1240 [heh]. Velten's 1899 data come from speakers of the Mkwawa court (Iringa/Kalenga); Odden's data (1980s-90s) from speakers John Mtenge and Margaret Fivawo. Odden 1988 treats 'Hibena' (Bena, bena1262) as a separate, tonally different but very close language; von Sowa 1900 'Ki-Bena (Ki-Hehe)' conflates the two and was not used.

new_statements.reading: Word accent on the first stem syllable (i.e. the syllable after the class prefix), with an additional final-syllable accent in four-syllable words; accented vowels are long. This is a 19th-century impressionistic 'Wortton' statement from Velten's elicitation with three Hehe speakers; later phonological work (Odden 1988; Odden 2005/2013; Kindole 2012 via Ngwasi 2021) describes Hehe as a tone language with lexical H and a penultimate-H rule and gives no stress rule, so the statement should be read as an early description of pitch prominence rather than a modern stress analysis. It remains the only explicit first-hand word-accent-placement statement for Hehe that was actually read in this sweep. The only sweep target (Möhlig 1969) could not be obtained.

sources.note: L2 Swahili transfer study (Swahili-medium): Hehe speakers put 'toni' with lengthening on the penult of Swahili words (/sama:ni/); says in Kihehe tone causes lengthened pronunciation of vowels. No word-stress rule for Kihehe.

sources.citation: Ngwasi, Lengson. 2021. The multiple functions of the reflexive prefix in Hehe, Sukuma, Nilamba, and Nyaturu. PhD diss., University of Gothenburg. Sec. 4.2.4 'Tone', pp.48-51, and 4.3.2.4.3.
sources.note: Hehe has lexical tone (gúla 'that' vs gula 'buy', after Kindole 2012) and grammatical tone (future tulíma = H on penultimate mora); infinitive prefix H (kúkama); H on penultimate mora of extended verbs (kúkamíla, kúkamilána, after Odden 2013:162-3). Nothing on stress.
